SBIR topic DON27BZ02-NV008 (Pre-Release); proposals open 2026-12-02; closes 2027-01-06.

Objective

Develop and demonstrate a ruggedized, multi-spectral imaging, 360-degree-capable camera system capable of integration into Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV) periscopes.

Description

Current periscopic vision systems on Marine Corps combat vehicles are limited to daylight optical performance, over a limited Field of View (FoV), and lack the ability to integrate modern digital imaging, thermal, and night vision technologies. The new system shall provide daylight, low-light/night vision, and thermal (IR) imaging capabilities through a single, compact, and modular unit; and enhance situational awareness, target detection, and crew safety for Marines during water, transition, and land operating environments.

This SBIR topic seeks to develop an integrated camera-based periscope module that:

Provides visible (Electro-Optical [EO]), night vision (Near-Infrared Low-Level Laser (or Light) [NIR/LLL]), and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imaging in a compact unit.

Is retrofit-compatible with existing periscope housings used in the USMC ACV FOV, or is capable of replacing optical viewports with an electronic display module.

Includes onboard image fusion and low-latency video output for vehicle displays and augmented-reality systems.

Meets ruggedization standards (MIL-STD-810H, MIL-STD-461D, and EC Standard 60529, rating IP66) for temperature, shock, vibration, EMI, dust and water resistance.

Objective

Develop tools and/or techniques to improve characterization of the D-region ionosphere sufficient for skillful ionosphere model specification and forecast over climatology and that demonstrate the impact of improved methodology on ionosphere accuracy for use by high frequency (HF) and very low frequency (VLF) signal propagation tools.

Description

HF and VLF skywave propagation depend on knowledge of the altitudinal structure of the ionosphere for reliable system operation. The D-region ionosphere, a region typically between 60-90 km altitude above the Earth’s surface, is particularly challenging to predict with sufficient fidelity for skywave mission planning because the region is difficult to measure with in situ measurements. Remote sensing methods provide a limited dataset from which to develop detailed physical and assimilative models that can reliably produce the regional behavior on a day-to-day basis.

Operational models like the D-Region Absorption Product (D-RAP) produce maps of outage areas as a function of radio frequency (RF) to inform HF system users of anticipated degradation or blackouts due to radiation increases. These predictions primarily address HF absorption due to solar X-ray flares at low and mid-latitudes and do not address the VLF propagation use case. Objective

Description

Objective

High-energy lasers integrated onto airborne platforms hold immense potential for a variety of applications, relevant to DAF missions. However, the demanding operational environments encountered by airborne systems, characterized by factors like vibration, shock, temperature fluctuations, and pressure variations, pose significant challenges to the performance and reliability of traditional optical systems. To achieve demanding pointing and line of sight stabilization requirements necessary for the laser to have the desired effect on target, a precision optical beam control system is required to sense and correct platform induced disturbances, acquire and track targets, and sense and compensate for atmospheric and aero-optical disturbances. Historically these optical systems are implemented on flat optical benches or breadboards, in a similar manner to a ground-based laboratory. To fully realize the potential of airborne laser systems, there is a critical need for innovative optical systems designed specifically for ruggedness and environmental stability. This research effort aims to develop and demonstrate a ruggedized, environmentally stable, and optimally packaged optical beam control system specifically tailored for airborne high-energy laser applications, in a more optimized form factor for an airborne system than a conventional flat optical bench or breadboard.

SBIR topic DON27BZ02-NV022 (Pre-Release); proposals open 2026-12-02; closes 2027-01-06.

Objective

Develop a collapsible, low-cost, fixed-wing Group 1 small uncrewed aerial system (sUAS) capable of autonomous intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions with a flight endurance of over one hour.

Description

The Navy has a growing need for a low-cost, portable, and rapidly deployable UAS to support ISR missions. Current systems are often expensive and bulky, and require significant logistical support. This SBIR topic seeks an innovative solution for a collapsible fixed-wing UAS that can be easily transported and deployed by a single operator. The UAS should be capable of autonomous flight and integration with standard flight control software (e.g., QGroundControl, Pixhawk).

Key requirements include a total cost under $5,000 for the airframe and components, a flight time exceeding one hour, a communication range of up to 10 km, and the ability to fit within a 2' x 2' x 1' case for transport. The system must support a modular nose payload, be initially equipped with an RGB camera, and have the potential to serve as a signal repeater for transmission of data. The primary technical challenge is to achieve the desired endurance and portability within the stringent cost constraints, requiring innovation in airframe design, materials, and component integration.

Objective

Develop a human-portable wave energy capture device able to deploy autonomously and generate sufficient power to effectively recharge autonomous vehicles.

Description

Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD). WECDs capture kinetic and potential energy generated by the movement of ocean waves on or near the surface of open water.

The desired WECD must be portable, specifically, designed as a set of components that can each be carried by one or two people who must be able to quickly assemble and disassemble those components. Components designed for one-person carry should weigh no more than 14 kg with largest dimension no greater than 1.9 m, while components designed for two-person carry should weigh no more than 45.4 kg with largest dimension no greater than 2.3 m. The WECD must be able to be relocated to areas of very different depths, including full ocean depth so the WECD’s design cannot require placement or anchoring on the sea floor. And since the WECD may need to deploy near the shore, its design must allow it to function in waters as shallow as 100 meters.

SBIR topic DAF27BZ01-NV001 (Open); closes 2026-11-25.

Objective

Create a physics-based engineering model solution for shallow fuel jet spurts

Description

This topic seeks the development of a computationally efficient engineering-level model to predict the formation and characteristics of the "spurt" in fluid cavity created jets. The hydrodynamic spurt is the initial, often unsteady, ejection of material from the liner, preceding the formation of the main, stable jet. Current hydrocodes can model this phenomenon but are computationally expensive and ill-suited for rapid design iteration. This project will develop a validated, reduced-order model that accurately predicts spurt velocity, mass, and geometry as a function of liner material, geometry, and threat characteristics, enabling faster design and optimization of advanced warheads.

It would provide detailed procedures and technical knowledge for diagnostics, repair and maintenance procedures on demand, both ashore and at sea, where there will be limited access to remote data stores. SBIR topic DAF27BZ02-DV025 (Pre-Release); proposals open 2026-12-02; closes 2027-01-06.

Objective

Wideband receivers used in electronic warfare (EW), signals intelligence (SigInt), and electronic support measures (ESM) need to instantaneously capture broad swaths of spectrum to avoid missing frequency agile radio frequency (RF) signals. Wideband receivers, however, lack the dynamic range to capture wide bandwidths of spectrum containing both large interferers and weak signals of interest. Thus, multiple receivers are needed in these applications which results in large size and power consumption.

Description

The objective of this topic is to develop miniature, low power, and high selectivity tunable notch filters capable of protecting wideband receivers from large interferers. The effort will target the largest interferers which are in L, S, C, and X bands with tunable notch filters, while allowing pass bandwidths spanning L through Ku bands. Each notch filter must be continuously tunable across a minimum of 3 of the 4 targeted bands (L, S, C, and X) while having a notch depth > 20 dB and a notch bandwidth < 1 % across all tuned frequencies. With a narrow notch bandwidth, each notch filter must be programmable and maintained with an accuracy of 50% of the notch bandwidth and should maintain this accuracy over temperature. The notch filters must be able to reject large interfering signals and therefore should be able to notch receive interference levels greater than 5 dBm.

Objective

Develop, integrate, and demonstrate a low-SWaP-C neuromorphic IR sensor to support celestial navigation to enable position and navigation of sUAS in a Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) denied environment in day and nighttime for world-wide operations. The desired system should allow an autonomous aircraft to establish a persistent machine representation of an area, recognize operationally meaningful changes, and communicate primarily what changed rather than continuously transmitting full-motion imagery or raw sensor data.

Description

Traditional airborne ISR architectures frequently collect and transmit large quantities of data even when little or nothing within the observed environment has changed. This creates substantial burdens on: Communications bandwidth. Processing. Storage. Power. Analysts. Command-and-control systems. Neuromorphic and event-driven sensors offer a fundamentally different sensing architecture in which the system responds primarily to changes within the observed environment.

Objective

The United States currently faces an "unprecedented" military buildup by China and increasing air and missile threats that demand a robust deterrent. However, the current inventory of long-range strike weapons is dominated by high-cost, low-volume systems or aging strategic assets like the Minuteman III, which dates back to the 1960s. The lack of a cost-effective, ground-launched payload delivery system prevents the Joint Force from achieving producibility at scale, leaving the U.S. vulnerable in high-intensity, multi-domain environments where high-end munitions would be rapidly depleted. The objective of this topic is to facilitate innovative research on low-cost, rapidly manufacturable, payload delivery systems.

Description

The Department of War (DoW) is pivotally shifting toward "affordable mass" to counter peer adversaries who are rapidly expanding their military capabilities. While hypersonic systems offer high speeds, their exorbitant costs, exceeding $50 million per round, limit the military's ability to achieve the "magazine depth" necessary for prolonged conflict. This project proposes a ground-based, non-hypersonic, long-range precision payload delivery system that leverages low-cost production methods and commercial technologies to provide a scalable, high-volume alternative that is a tenth of the price of current high-end munitions. Objective

Design, fabricate, and experimentally test a wideband antenna solution ready to be integrated with standard RF-photonics transceiver modules. The antenna module must satisfy two key requirements. First, they should be fully compatible with standard packaging assemblies of RF-photonic modules. Second, they must deliver stable and efficient performance across a broad frequency bandwidth. SBIR topic OSW27BZ02-DV003 (Pre-Release); proposals open 2026-12-02; closes 2027-01-06.

Objective

Design, develop and demonstrate an innovative 5G/6Gdual-use Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC) prototype that provides sensing capabilities without degrading communication performance.

Description

The Department of War (DoW) seeks to accelerate U.S. leadership in Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC), a 5G-Advanced feasibility-study area and a key technology for 3GPP 6G specifications. This project addresses the challenge of adding sensing capabilities to communication networks without degrading the primary communication link across diverse missions and environments, from established bases to remote and contested areas. The goal is to develop innovative, dual-use ISAC prototypes that leverage existing cellular infrastructure including 5G, emerging Open RAN interfaces, and AI-native networking. These solutions should offer a smaller, more cost-effective footprint than separate radar and communication systems. The effort will focus on three pathways: ISAC on fixed infrastructure, ISAC on mobile platforms, and joint AI optimization of radio resources. Success of this project will reduce barriers to market entry, enable new ISAC and AI applications, and strengthen U.S. industrial competitiveness in a field receiving substantial investment from adversaries.

Objective

1- Develop a platform agnostic fully autonomous Agentic SI swarm system suitable for multidomain naval operations (i.e., Sea, Air, Space, Land, and Cyber) with self-awareness for rapid operationally scalable response, namely “hyper-scalability”. The Agentic SI system, a hybrid-evolutionary SI, must self-replicate and self-deploy. As a team, it must autonomously reason to scale-up or scale-down its swarming clusters to generate tactical sub-clusters or end-game sub-clusters for defensive and offensive measures to confront and overwhelm threats. Neuro-Symbolic SI is to be a practical method for these SI-based swarm agents to explore and exploit the conditions in the operational ecosystem.

Objective

Develop an inexpensive, compact, and National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)-compliant Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) - optimized for marine mammal monitoring.

Description

A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations. Advances in UAS methods and technology present unprecedented opportunities to improve the capacity to collect this robust data with minimal disturbance to marine species. This encompasses novel instrumentation necessary for the coming era of AI-driven discoveries. This pilot will prioritize investing in the necessary infrastructure to support entirely new fields of scientific discovery, making new technological breakthroughs and transformative applications possible. Through this approach, NSF will continue to lead in propelling the scientific enterprise to new frontiers.

Description:

The U.S. Army, through the Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD) and U.S. Army Europe and Africa (USAREUR-AF), in operational partnership with the U.S. Army FUZE xTech Program, is conducting an Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) to evaluate, demonstrate, and acquire operationally mature (TRL 6+) electromagnetic spectrum operations (EMSO) capabilities.

This effort enables U.S. Army forces operating within a North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and joint coalition framework on the Eastern Flank to sense, understand, exploit, attack, and protect across a contested electromagnetic environment (EME) and connected cyberspace. To preserve combat power and freedom of maneuver, forces must protect tactical command and control (C2) networks while delivering synchronized lethal and non-lethal effects at depth against adversary systems.

This is an informational Special Notice only. It does not constitute a Request for Proposal (RFP), a formal Request for Information (RFI), or an invitation for bid. The official prize competition, including all cash prize allocations, evaluation criteria, and challenge rules, is administered exclusively through the external xTech platform.
